title: How Do Habits Form?
paragraphs: A considerable share of everyday conduct is less the outcome of deliberation than of habit. Preparing breakfast, reaching for a phone or retracing the familiar commute proceed with scant conscious oversight, an economy that spares limited cognitive resources for circumstances that are genuinely novel.

Researchers commonly model habits as a loop of cue, routine and reward. The cue may be a time of day, a setting, a mood or a preceding action; the routine is the behaviour proper; and the reward is whatever consequence consolidates the association and predisposes the organism to repeat it.

With sufficient repetition, control of the behaviour seems to shift from neural circuitry associated with goal-directed planning towards systems that underpin automatic responding. Thereafter the cue may elicit the routine largely irrespective of whether the reward remains desirable, a dissociation that goes some way towards explaining both the tenacity of unwanted habits and the notorious inadequacy of resolve as a remedy.

The acquisition of new habits is, accordingly, a slow affair. A much-cited study at University College London reported a mean of 66 days before a daily behaviour attained automaticity, albeit with striking variation between participants. The more promising interventions thus privilege design over exhortation: starting with deliberately modest steps, yoking the new routine to an established cue and restructuring one’s surroundings so that the desired behaviour becomes the path of least resistance.
